definition: Microsoft's published commitment for an Azure service: a monthly uptime percentage, the configurations it applies to, and the service credit paid if it is missed. It is a financial promise rather than a guarantee, and free, shared and some single-instance tiers have no SLA at all.
example: App Service on a Standard or Premium plan carries a 99.95% monthly SLA; the F1 free plan carries none.

definition: The availability of a whole system worked out from the SLAs of its parts. Services in series multiply (each must be up), so the result is always below the weakest link; redundant copies in parallel combine as 1 − (1−a)(1−b), which raises it.
example: Front Door 99.99% × App Service 99.95% × Azure SQL 99.99% ≈ 99.93%, or about 31 minutes a month.

definition: Shorthand for an availability percentage by counting the nines: 99.9% is three nines, 99.99% is four. Each extra nine allows roughly a tenth of the downtime and, in practice, costs far more than ten times the engineering.
example: Three nines allows 43.8 minutes of downtime a month; four nines allows 4.4 minutes.

definition: The maximum amount of data loss a business can accept after a failure, expressed as time. An RPO of 15 minutes means replication or backups must never be more than 15 minutes behind. A nightly backup implies an RPO of 24 hours.
example: Azure SQL geo-replication keeps the secondary a few seconds behind, well inside the shop's 15-minute RPO.

definition: The maximum time a service may be unavailable after a failure before it must be running again. Meeting an RTO depends less on the technology than on whether the failover has been rehearsed.
example: An RTO of 1 hour for the ordering API, tested by a quarterly failover to the paired region.

definition: Microsoft's set of design principles for Azure workloads, organised into five pillars: Reliability, Security, Cost Optimization, Operational Excellence and Performance Efficiency. Used as a design-review checklist; Azure Advisor reports findings against the same pillars.
example: The team walks the five pillars in every design review, asking one question per pillar.

definition: Running more than one copy of a component so that one can fail without an outage. Copies can be within a data centre (instance), across availability zones (zone) or across regions (region); each level protects against a bigger failure and costs more.
example: Two App Service instances across zones mean a host reboot no longer takes the API down.

definition: Designing a service to keep running through component failures - a VM dying, a host being patched, a zone losing power - without an outage, usually through redundancy within a region. It does not protect against the whole region being lost; that is disaster recovery.
example: A zone-redundant Azure SQL database stays online while one availability zone is offline.

definition: The plan and mechanisms for recovering a service in another region when the primary region is unavailable: replicated data, a second deployment, and a rehearsed failover measured against RPO and RTO. A backup alone is not disaster recovery.
example: Geo-replication to the paired region plus a quarterly failover drill that must complete within the one-hour RTO.

definition: The refund Microsoft gives when a service misses its SLA in a month: a percentage of that month's charge for that service, rising with the size of the miss, and usually claimed rather than paid automatically. It is capped at what you paid, so it never covers the business cost of an outage.
example: A month at 99.0% on a service with a 99.95% SLA earns a 10% credit on that service's bill - perhaps £30.

definition: A system's ability to keep working, or recover quickly, when parts of it fail or misbehave. It combines redundancy, transient fault handling, graceful degradation and rehearsed recovery. The Reliability pillar of the Well-Architected Framework is largely about resiliency.
example: When the recommendations service is down, the shop still shows the product page without the 'you may also like' panel.

definition: A short-lived failure - a dropped connection, a throttled request, a database failing over - that succeeds if retried a moment later. Cloud services expect them; applications must retry with back-off rather than treat every error as fatal.
example: The Node API retries a SQL connection three times with increasing delays before returning an error.
